title: Alms and Ale
text:
Research question
Building on Malthus’s insight that subsidized populations may shift consumption toward leisure and intoxicants, this project asks whether more generous welfare provision inadvertently increases the demand for “vice” goods such as alcohol. The approach assembles a multi-decade panel of OECD countries (1995–2023) and estimates fixed-effects, instrumental-variable, and dynamic specifications that control for income, taxation, culture, and time trends.

title: Private Mechanisms for Stopping Diamond-Dybvig Runs
text: Working paper · with Daniel J. Smith

title: Private Mechanisms for Stopping Diamond-Dybvig Runs
text:
Overview
To what extent did U.S. banks and their communities develop private mechanisms to combat Diamond-Dybvig bank runs? Using digitized historical newspapers, we construct a novel dataset of 544 bank runs reported between 1889 and 1929 — spanning the National Banking Era through the early Federal Reserve — and systematically code the strategies banks and communities used to stop them. Beyond the familiar tools (suspension of redemption, clearinghouse assistance, disclosure, management turnover), we document detailed narrative evidence on eight understudied but commonly deployed mechanisms, suggesting private order offered a more robust defense against runs than the canonical model implies.

title: Private Mechanisms for Stopping Diamond-Dybvig Runs
text:
Abstract

“To what extent did U.S. banks and their communities develop private mechanisms to combat Diamond-Dybvig bank runs? Using digitized historical newspapers, we construct a novel dataset of 544 bank runs reported between 1889 and 1929. We systematically code the mitigation strategies employed by banks and their communities. We confirm the widespread use of several mechanisms previously discussed in the literature, including suspension of redemption, clearinghouse assistance, information disclosure, and management turnover. In addition, we provide detailed narrative evidence on eight understudied but commonly deployed mechanisms: (1) non-invocation of redemption clauses, (2) forfeiture of interest, (3) passbook speculation, (4) direct loans from other financial institutions, (5) assurances from prominent community, business, financial, and governmental actors, (6) prominent displays of reserves, (7) modified banking hours, and (8) expanded clearinghouse roles. The findings suggest that private mechanisms offered a more robust defense against Diamond-Dybvig runs than the canonical model implies, in addition to, or even in the absence of, deposit insurance or a fully developed lender of last resort.”

title: Private Mechanisms for Stopping Diamond-Dybvig Runs
text:
Headline findings

544 bank runs identified from digitized newspapers, 1889–1929; 390 employed at least one private mitigation mechanism.
A companion paper, “Bank Runs without a Cause,” isolates 273 no-cause runs: roughly 79% were averted in an average of 2.2 days, and only 5 spread beyond the initial bank.
The most common responses were market-based — external loans and reserves, credible disclosure, and assurances from prominent local figures — not government backstops.

title: Crisis and Local Leviathan
text: Work in progress · sole-authored

title: Crisis and Local Leviathan
text:
The question
Robert Higgs’s Crisis and Leviathan argues that emergencies permanently enlarge government: a crisis legitimates new spending, agencies, and powers; the crisis passes; the government stays. The evidence for the ratchet is federal (war, depression, the New Deal), and in each of those episodes the government doing the growing was one its citizens could not escape.
This paper asks whether the ratchet survives the removal of that condition. Local governments face real emergencies, but their residents can move across the county line, and much of their disaster money arrives from Washington and the state capital. If the ratchet is a general property of government under stress, it should appear here too. If it depends on insulation from exit, it should weaken or vanish.

title: Crisis and Local Leviathan
text:
The design
The current revision uses hurricane-force wind as the crisis. A metro is treated in the first year, 1988–2012, in which population-weighted sustained winds reach hurricane strength, and each struck metro is compared with unstruck metros in the same state. The outcomes are the annual budgets of county, municipal, and township governments (intergovernmental aid, operating spending, and taxes, alone and relative to local income) and the U.S. Metropolitan Area Economic Freedom Index. A broader sample of all large natural-disaster losses serves as a cross-check.

title: Research
text: My research program asks a single question across very different historical and institutional settings: when does regulation actually serve the public interest, and when is it better understood as protection for incumbents, a tool of bureaucratic expansion, or a substitute for order that markets and communities already provide? A newer line of work turns the same lens on the size of government itself, asking when crisis actually enlarges the state and when competition between jurisdictions prevents it. I combine historical institutional analysis with modern econometric and panel-data methods, in the tradition of Buchanan, Tullock, and Stigler and the Austrian emphasis on knowledge problems and spontaneous order.

title: Research
text:
Dissertation
My dissertation develops this question through three essays.

Distillers and Chemists: Strategic Capture of the Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897
Job market paper · sole-authored
The Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897 is conventionally remembered as one of America’s first consumer-protection laws. I read it instead as a government-administered credence-goods certification that the incumbent straight distillers could not supply privately. Using a newly digitized state-by-fiscal-year panel from the Commissioner of Internal Revenue’s annual reports, I find the Act did not foreclose the rival rectifier trade: the straight–rectified gap narrowed by about 23 percent. Instead it created a certified segment that grew from 0.54 million gallons in 1898 to 4.79 million by 1908, and Kentucky and Pennsylvania took 92 percent of its withdrawals over 1898–1904. A regulation can genuinely certify quality and still redistribute toward the incumbents who design it.
Summary & figures Draft available on request


Private Mechanisms for Stopping Diamond-Dybvig Runs: Evidence from U.S. Newspapers, 1889–1929
with Daniel J. Smith
Assembling a new dataset of 544 bank runs hand-coded from digitized newspapers, we document how localized runs were contained by a rich toolkit of private, market-based mechanisms, eight of them understudied. The evidence qualifies the standard case for deposit insurance and a fully developed lender of last resort.
Summary & figures Companion paper (SSRN)


Who Killed the Green Fairy? Temperance, Language, and Wine in the Swiss Absinthe Ban of 1908
with Nicholas A. Jensen
Switzerland’s 1908 vote to ban absinthe is usually read as a temperance triumph. Using canton-level records of both the petition and the vote, we find that organized temperance carried the petition while the wine interest appears at the ballot: holding the French-speaking share fixed, a one-point higher share of national wine revenue goes with a 0.62-point higher yes-share. The same specification finds no wine effect on six unrelated federal ballots.
Download Paper (PDF) Summary & figures

title: Research
text:
Beyond the dissertation
The projects beyond the dissertation carry the same question into new terrain: whether crisis actually enlarges the state, what the repeal of a legal regime reveals about who it protected, and how the welfare state interacts with the vices it is said to subsidize.

Uncorked: How Wall Street Priced the Repeal of Prohibition
with Patricia Hummel and Corey Pendleton
How did equity markets price the end of Prohibition? Dating the moments investors learned of repeal from newspaper coverage of the 1933 ratification process, we estimate abnormal returns for alcohol firms and related industries. Alcohol stocks rose when New York voted to send repeal delegates, then fell sharply in July once Alabama, Arkansas, and Tennessee made repeal certain, while most other industries barely moved. Investors priced repeal as the end of a protected market: competition would return and erode the profits the surviving firms had earned under Prohibition.
A companion paper builds a hand-verified dataset of distillery entry and enforcement events from New York newspapers, 1929–1940: 697 distinct events from 1,681 candidate hits, 677 of them enforcement actions against illicit stills and just 20 legal entries.
Summary Draft available on request


Crisis and Local Leviathan
Work in progress · sole-authored
This project moves from particular regulations to the size of government itself. It tests Robert Higgs’s ratchet hypothesis, that emergencies permanently enlarge the state, at the level of American government where exit is cheapest. The current revision follows the annual budgets of county and city governments in metropolitan areas struck by hurricane-force winds, compared with unstruck metros in the same state, alongside the metropolitan economic freedom index.
Project summary


Alms and Ale
A further project asks whether more generous welfare states raise the demand for alcohol, using a panel of OECD countries, 1995–2023.

title: Who Killed the Green Fairy?
text:
Working paper · with Nicholas A. Jensen (Wabash College)
Download Paper (PDF)

title: Who Killed the Green Fairy?
text:
Abstract

On July 5, 1908, Swiss voters wrote a ban on absinthe into their federal constitution, the first national prohibition of the drink enacted by popular vote. The temperance movement led the campaign. Deputies and historians pointed to the wine industry, which stood to gain if drinkers switched to wine, but no one has measured its part. We measure it across 25 cantons at both stages: the petition that put the ban on the ballot, and the vote. The Protestant share, our measure of organized temperance, predicts signatures per hundred eligible voters; the wine share does not. At the vote, the raw returns hide wine’s part: the wine-growing cantons tended to be French-speaking, and French-speaking cantons gave the ban less support. Holding the French-speaking share fixed, a one-percentage-point higher share of national wine revenue goes with a 0.620-point higher yes-share. Both estimates are significant at five percent under all four of our small-sample inference procedures. Under the same specification, wine has no detectable effect on six unrelated ballots and is positive, at ten percent by permutation test, on the 1906 food-law referendum, where wine was again at stake. Temperance carried the petition; the wine interest appears at the ballot, as a beneficiary rather than a leader.

JEL codes: N43 · D72 · L66 · I18

title: Who Killed the Green Fairy?
text:
The question
The ban passed with 63.5 percent of the vote and carried every canton except Neuchâtel and Geneva, over the Federal Council’s own recommendation to reject it. The temperance societies ran the campaign, and their case rested on “absinthism,” a disease said to be distinct from ordinary drunkenness. Modern analysis finds nothing in pre-ban absinthe, at obtainable doses, that sets it apart from chronic alcohol abuse.
Contemporaries also noticed who stood to gain. Absinthe had spread as a cheap substitute for wine, and the Alcohol Administration’s own expert predicted that other drinks “would take the place of the prohibited absinthe.” Deputies and historians have pointed at the wine trade ever since, but no one had taken the claim to the data. This is, to our knowledge, the first quantitative analysis of the vote.
The initiative left two canton-level records. The petition that put the ban on the ballot (167,814 valid signatures, the largest count then recorded) captures organized mobilization, because signing was voluntary. The vote captures the electorate at large. We estimate each across the 25 cantons, holding the French-speaking share fixed, and check every estimate with four small-sample inference procedures, among them a Freedman–Lane permutation test.

title: Who Killed the Green Fairy?
text:
Preliminary results

The petition belonged to temperance. Signatures per hundred eligible voters rise with the Protestant share, our measure of standing temperance organization (0.174, SE 0.065). The wine share is indistinguishable from zero.
The vote is where wine appears. In the raw returns the wine–yes relationship runs the wrong way, because the wine-growing cantons were mostly French-speaking and French-speaking cantons supported the ban less. Among cantons equally French-speaking, a one-point higher share of national wine revenue goes with a 0.620-point higher yes-share (SE 0.232).
Wine shows up only where wine was at stake. On six federal ballots from 1897–1908 that had nothing to do with drink, the wine coefficient sits near zero. It turns positive again on the 1906 food-law referendum, where the wine trade had a direct stake (permutation p = .083).
The reading. Temperance led the campaign; the wine interest followed at the ballot, where a vote could track local economic interest at little cost. The evidence supports wine as the ban’s predicted beneficiary, not as a co-conspirator at the petition stage.

text:

Points are least-squares estimates with 90 percent Bell–McCaffrey intervals; dotted lines separate the six falsification votes, the corroborating votes, and the 1908 absinthe vote (#68). Data
The canton-level dataset combines the federal returns for the 1908 vote and nine other referenda (1897–1908), the canton signature counts for the 1906–07 petition, wine harvest volume and revenue by canton, the Federal Alcohol Administration’s 1907 register of absinthe houses (verified house by house against the sources), and census measures of language, confession, tavern employment, and population density.

title: Distillers and Chemists: Strategic Capture of the Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897
text: Job market paper · sole-authored

title: Distillers and Chemists: Strategic Capture of the Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897
text:
Overview
The Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897 is usually remembered as one of America’s first consumer-protection laws — a federal guarantee, in an age of rampant adulteration, that what the label promised was what the bottle held. This paper reads the Act through public choice instead: as a government-administered solution to a credence-goods problem the straight distillers of Kentucky and Pennsylvania could not solve privately. Their brands and marks were freely counterfeited down a distribution chain they could not police; a Treasury strip stamp, backed by federal criminal law, made their quality signal excludable in a way no private mark ever had.
The reframing yields a sharp, testable distinction. If the Act worked by raising rivals’ costs, certified output should have grown at the expense of the rectifiers (blenders of cheaper neutral spirit) and a scarcity rent should have opened in relative prices. If it worked by certifying quality, a new premium tier should have grown from a near-zero base without the rectifying trade falling. The two mechanisms make opposite predictions — and the data can tell them apart.
The evidence comes from a newly digitized state-by-fiscal-year panel built from the Annual Reports of the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, FY1877–1920 — whiskey deposited into bond, tax-paid withdrawals, spirits rectified, distilleries operated, grain consumed, and (after 1897) withdrawals under the bottled-in-bond stamp — validated against the printed totals through 459 cross-year chain assertions and 59 zero-tolerance national control totals.

title: Distillers and Chemists: Strategic Capture of the Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897
text:
Abstract

“The Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897 allowed whiskey to be sold under a federal strip stamp certifying it as the unblended product of a single distillery and season, aged four years in a government-supervised bonded warehouse. Conventionally read as consumer protection, the Act was a government-administered credence-goods certification. Using a newly digitized state-by-fiscal-year panel built from the reports of the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, I estimate a common-treatment-date event study and difference-in-differences and find no foreclosure of the rectifier trade: rectified output grew at least as fast as straight whiskey after 1897, and the straight-minus-rectified gap narrows rather than widens, a contrast conditional on a pre-period in which the gap was already narrowing. Instead the Act created a certified segment that grew from a near-zero base—slowly at first, then rapidly as demand was cultivated—with rents concentrated among incumbent Kentucky and Pennsylvania producers. Capture operated not by raising rivals’ costs but through who collected the segment’s rents.”

title: Distillers and Chemists: Strategic Capture of the Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897
text:
A preview of the findings
1. No foreclosure. Indexed to 1896, rectified output reaches 186 by 1905 against straight whiskey’s 181 — the trade the bill’s proponents complained of grew at least as fast as the trade the Act favored. The within-state difference-in-differences on the straight–rectified gap runs the wrong way for foreclosure — the gap narrows by about 23% (−0.258, se 0.148) on the full one-definition FY1887–1908 panel, whose pre-trends pass on every window — and at ninety-five percent one-sided the design rules out any post-Act widening at all.
2. A manufactured premium segment. The genuine expansion is the certified sub-segment itself: bottled-in-bond withdrawals grew from 0.54 million gallons in 1898 to 4.79 million by 1908 — flat through FY1902, then accelerating sharply as demand was cultivated — reaching about 3 percent of straight output by 1905, a small tier expanding on top of an existing trade. Whether that volume was new or relabeled is the question the quantity record leaves open: within adopting states the elasticity of non-bonded on bonded volume is −0.185 (se 0.073), inside the band that one-for-one relabeling implies at the observed bonded shares. The prices speak more clearly. A hedonic model of hand-collected quotes attaches a ~10% premium to the bonded label, conditional on age and channel, while the certifiable–rectified price gap does not widen — the price pattern a quality-signaling mechanism predicts and a scarcity-rent mechanism does not.
3. Rents captured by design. Kentucky and Pennsylvania together supplied 92.1% of all bonded withdrawals over 1898–1904, with the Louisville collection district — home market of the Act’s chief proponent, E. H. Taylor Jr. — taking 28 percent of the national total in 1905 alone. And the concentration was targeting by design: over FY1898–1908, Kentucky’s share of bonded withdrawals equals its share of aged stocks in bond (0.99×) — the statute’s four-year bonding requirement attached the subsidy to the aging inventory the incumbents already held, while Pennsylvania’s 1.38× marks the discretionary margin above the designed transfer. The demand for certified whiskey was actively cultivated by Harvey Wiley’s federal purity chemists, whose authority the distillers enrolled to teach buyers to distrust uncertified spirit. The mechanism is credence-segment creation; the distribution is geographic rent capture.
The upshot: capture need not look like foreclosure. A regulation can expand a market, resolve a real information asymmetry, and still function as capture through who collects the rents it manufactures.

title: Uncorked
text: Working paper · with Patricia Hummel and Corey Pendleton

title: Uncorked
text:
Abstract

This paper examines how equity markets priced the repeal of Alcohol Prohibition in 1933. We estimate abnormal returns for alcohol firms and firms in related industries, including tobacco, soft drinks, sugar refining, confectionery, drugs, machinery, warehousing, and retail. This paper uses newspaper articles during key events in the repeal process to identify when investors received and incorporated new information into their trades, then estimates abnormal returns using CAPM, Fama-French three-factor, and Carhart four-factor models. Alcohol stocks rose considerably when New York voted to send delegates to repeal the Eighteenth Amendment, but the largest response came in July after results in Alabama, Arkansas, and Tennessee made repeal a certainty. Alcohol stocks fell sharply, whereas most other industries experienced much smaller or mixed responses. This pattern is consistent with investors expecting repeal to restore competition to the alcohol market and erode the supernormal profits earned by surviving alcohol firms during Prohibition.

title: Uncorked
text:
Design
Under Prohibition, legal alcohol production was confined to a small set of surviving firms and was largely medicinal. The paper dates the moments investors learned repeal was coming from newspaper coverage of the ratification process, then estimates abnormal returns around those dates for alcohol firms and for firms in related industries (tobacco, soft drinks, sugar refining, confectionery, drugs, machinery, warehousing, and retail) under CAPM, Fama-French three-factor, and Carhart four-factor benchmarks.

title: Uncorked
text:
Findings

New York’s vote moved alcohol stocks up. Alcohol stocks rose considerably when New York voted to send delegates to repeal the Eighteenth Amendment.
Certainty moved them down. The largest response came in July 1933, after results in Alabama, Arkansas, and Tennessee made repeal a certainty: alcohol stocks fell sharply.
Related industries barely moved. Most other industries show much smaller or mixed responses.
The reading. Investors priced repeal as the end of a protected market, one that would restore competition and erode the supernormal profits the surviving firms had earned during Prohibition.

title: Uncorked
text:
Companion project: entry and enforcement
A second paper with the same coauthors builds the measurement behind the entry margin: a hand-verified dataset of distillery entry and enforcement events from New York newspapers, 1929–1940. From 1,681 candidate newspaper hits, each read against the original page image, it distills 697 distinct events (677 enforcement actions against illicit stills and just 20 legal entries). Verification is the contribution: an unverified keyword count would overstate legal entry by a factor of roughly fourteen.

title: Teaching
text:
My decision to earn a Ph.D. in economics was driven first and foremost by a desire to teach. As a student at Hampden-Sydney College, I experienced small, discussion-oriented classes in which professors invested deeply in their students’ intellectual growth — courses that permanently changed how I see the world. My central goal is to help students acquire a lasting economic way of thinking: understanding incentives, trade-offs, opportunity costs, and unintended consequences. Because business students want to know “how this applies,” I anchor every major concept in concrete, real-world examples — price controls during shortages, the economics of ride-sharing regulation, minimum-wage effects, the logic behind payday lending — and tie them to the empirical literature.
I work to create a classroom that is clear, supportive, and interactive: pausing often to check for questions, walking through graphs carefully, and using short Kahoot reviews and end-of-class activities that students say help them learn the most. Economics inevitably touches on contested moral and political questions; my aim is never to hand students a set of policy conclusions, but to give them the analytical tools to reach their own.
